## What is a Bloom filter? {background-image="figures/static/bloom1970.png" background-size="contain" background-position="right" background-opacity="0.5"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Published in 1970 by Burton H. Bloom
- A space-efficient, probabilistic set data structure
- False positives are possible; false negatives are not
- Trades a small error rate for significantly less memory usage
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- How many people know or have used Bloom filter(s)?
- The original paper:
  - Bloom worked at Computer Usage Company in Massachusetts. The paper is about hash coding when memory is too small to hold the data.
  - He analyzed three competing factors: hash area size (space), time to reject a non-member ("reject time"), and an allowable error rate.
  - The target: applications where most of the tested items are *not* in the set, so the fast "no" matters most.
  - The idea: accept a small fraction of false "yes" answers ("errors of commission") to fit the hash area in core memory, and catch those errors with a slower secondary check.
  - His example: automatic hyphenation of a 500,000-word dictionary. 90% of words follow simple rules; 10% need a disk lookup. The in-memory filter holds those 10%.
  - Result: a hash area 18% of the size of an error-free one still eliminates 87% of the disk accesses.
:::
